pericopes.text: Behold, it came to pass that I, Omni, being commanded by my father Jarom, that I should write somewhat upon these plates, to preserve our genealogy;

wherefore, in my days, I would that ye should know that I fought much with the sword, to preserve my people, the Nephites, from falling into the hands of their enemies, the Lamanites. But behold, I, of myself, am a wicked man; and I have not kept the statutes and the commandments of the Lord, as I ought to have done.

And it came to pass that two hundred and seventy and six years had passed away, and we had many seasons of peace; and we had many seasons of serious war and bloodshed.—Yea, and in fine, two hundred and eighty and two years had passed away, and I had kept these plates according to the commandments of my fathers; and I conferred them upon my son Amaron. And I make an end.
And now I, Amaron, write the things whatsoever I write, which are few, in the book of my father.
Behold, it came to pass that three hundred and twenty years had passed away, and the more wicked part of the Nephites were destroyed:

for the Lord would not suffer, after he had led them out of the land of Jerusalem, and kept and preserved them from falling into the hands of their enemies; yea, he would not suffer that the words should not be verified, which he spake unto our fathers, saying, That inasmuch as ye will not keep my commandments, ye shall not prosper in the land.

provenance.route: 1 Kings 9:6-7 → KJV → 1 Nephi 2:20-21 → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “will not keep my commandments” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 9:6; the KJV's ordinary negative is 'if ye will not hearken unto me' (Leviticus 26:14) or 'if thou wilt not observe to do all the words of this law' (Deuteronomy 28:58). The Book of Mormon's land-covenant is stated positively at 1 Nephi 2:20 ('inasmuch as ye shall keep my commandments, ye shall prosper in the land of promise') and thereafter cited as a fixed formula. Omni 1:6 is the first place in the book where the formula is quoted in its NEGATIVE form and immediately cashed out in a narrative of destruction, which is exactly the shape of 1 Kings 9:6-7.
provenance.significance: This is a mediation finding rather than a verbal one. Amaleki's source is not the Bible directly but the Lehi covenant of 1 Nephi 2, and the whole point of the sentence is that a promise made two centuries earlier is now being 'verified' against a people. The KJV supplies the grammar for that operation only once: Solomon's temple, where a conditional grant of land is spoken and its negative clause ('if ye shall at all turn from following me … and will not keep my commandments … Then will I cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them') is fulfilled in the historian's own narration. Omni 1:5-7 compresses that whole Deuteronomistic arc — condition, breach, judgement, preserved remnant — into three verses of a scribal colophon.

links.note: 'That inasmuch as ye will not keep my commandments, ye shall not prosper in the land.' The five-word run 'will not keep my commandments' is 1 Kings 9:6's; the machine stream found it and nothing else. What makes it worth cataloguing rather than dismissing as Deuteronomic boilerplate is that the surrounding verse reproduces 1 Kings 9's logic and not Deuteronomy's: the condition is attached to a specific land already given, the breach is narrated as history rather than warned of as future, and the consequence is being cut off from the land rather than the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28. Note that Omni's proximate model is a Book of Mormon text, not a biblical one — 1 Nephi 2:20 is where the promise is made, and Omni 1:6 quotes it back with the polarity reversed. The mediation call records that.
links.text: But if ye shall at all turn from following me, ye or your children, and will not keep my commandments and my statutes which I have set before you, but go and serve other gods, and worship them:

provenance.other: “words be verified” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 42:20. The verb itself is nearly as rare: 'verified' occurs in only three verses in the whole Bible — Genesis 42:20, 1 Kings 8:26, and its duplicate at 2 Chronicles 6:17 — and in two of the three the thing verified is a divine promise about a land and a dynasty.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the two halves of Omni 1:6 turn out to come from the two halves of one episode. 1 Kings 8:26 is Solomon asking that the word spoken to David 'be verified'; 1 Kings 9:6-7 is the Lord's answer, and it is the condition under which the same word is void. Amaleki has the prayer and the answer in a single sentence, and in the KJV's order: the Lord 'would not suffer that the words should not be verified, which he spake unto our fathers' (8:26), 'that inasmuch as ye will not keep my commandments, ye shall not prosper in the land' (9:6-7). The double negative in Omni is doing real work — it makes the destruction of the more wicked part of the Nephites an act of divine fidelity rather than of wrath.

links.note: 'He would not suffer that the words should not be verified, which he spake unto our fathers.' 'Verified' is not a common English Bible word and it is not a Book of Mormon word either; this is one of very few occurrences. The KJV uses it three times, and 1 Kings 8:26 — 'let thy word, I pray thee, be verified, which thou spakest unto thy servant David my father' — matches Omni's syntax down to the relative clause: verified + which + spake + unto + a named forefather. Genesis 42:20 supplies the only occurrence of the exact string, and is worth naming in provenance because it makes 'verified' the word for a test imposed on brothers who had sold one of their own; Omni 1:5-7 is a fratricidal war adjudicated by a promise. But 1 Kings 8:26 is the source, because it is the only one of the three where the words verified are a covenant about a land.
links.text: And now, O God of Israel, let thy word, I pray thee, be verified, which thou spakest unto thy servant David my father.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, the Lord did visit them in great judgment; nevertheless, he did spare the righteous, that they should not perish, but did deliver them out of the hands of their enemies.
And it came to pass that I did deliver the plates unto my brother Chemish.

Now I, Chemish, write what few things I write, in the same book with my brother: for behold, I saw the last which he wrote, that he wrote it with his own hand; and he wrote it in the day that he delivered them unto me. And after this manner we keep the records: for it is according to the commandments of our fathers. And I make an end.

Behold, I, Abinadom, I am the son of Chemish. Behold, it came to pass that I saw much war and contention between my people, the Nephites, and the Lamanites; and I, with mine own sword, have taken the lives of many of the Lamanites, in the defence of my brethren.

And behold, the record of this people is engraven upon plates which is had by the kings, according to the generations; and I know of no revelation, save that which has been written, neither prophecy; wherefore, that which is sufficient, is written. And I make an end.

provenance.other: “no open vision” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Bible has no other formula for a drought of revelation stated as a bare narrative fact; Amos 8:11-12 has a famine of hearing the word, and Psalm 74:9 'there is no more any prophet', but neither is placed where 1 Samuel 3:1 places it.
provenance.significance: The placement is the argument. 1 Samuel 3:1 says there was no open vision, and the next verse begins the call of Samuel — the drought is announced only so that its ending can be narrated. Abinadom's 'I know of no revelation, save that which has been written, neither prophecy' is the last sentence of the last of the four minimal colophons, and the very next verse opens Amaleki's account of a man 'warned of the Lord' who leads a people out and a king who reads an unknown script 'by the gift and power of God'. Whether or not Abinadom's editor knew he was doing it, the book uses 1 Samuel 3:1's structural device: silence declared, then broken.

links.note: Abinadom's whole contribution is a disclaimer — the record is with the kings, he has seen war, he knows of no revelation and no prophecy, what is sufficient is written. There is no verbal contact with 1 Samuel 3:1 beyond the shared idea, which is why this is an echo and not an allusion. The case rests on rarity plus position: the KJV states a revelatory drought outright exactly once, and it does so as the hinge into the call of a prophet, which is what Omni 1:11 is as well. Compare Hays on metalepsis — the meaning here lives entirely in the suppressed half of the source, the verse that follows.
links.whyNot: Nothing verbal is shared. 'Revelation' and 'prophecy' are Amaleki's editorial vocabulary throughout, and a reader could reasonably say Abinadom is simply reporting that he has nothing to add, in the same register as Chemish's 'what few things I write'. The link is recorded because the structural coincidence is exact and free to check, not because the wording compels it.
links.text: And the child Samuel ministered unto the LORD before Eli. And the word of the LORD was precious in those days; there was no open vision.

pericopes.text: Behold, I am Amaleki, the son of Abinadom. Behold, I will speak unto you somewhat concerning Mosiah, which was made king over the land of Zarahemla: for behold, he being warned of the Lord that he should flee out of the land of Nephi, and as many as would hearken unto the voice of the Lord, should also depart out of the land with him, into the wilderness.

provenance.other: “made king over” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The KJV's ordinary idioms are 'made him king' (2 Samuel 2:9), 'reigned over', and 'king of'; the passive participle governing 'over' plus a territory is Daniel 9:1's alone.
provenance.significance: The 1830 reading is the evidence. Omni 1:12 reads 'Mosiah, which was made king over the land of Zarahemla' — a six-word run, 'which was made king over the', reproducing Daniel 9:1's 'which was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans' exactly. The 1920 edition changed 'which' to 'who' as part of its general grammatical smoothing, and in doing so erased the run at its first word. This is CONVENTIONS §8 in its purest form: the borrowing is visible in the first edition and invisible in the modern text. It is also the first of two Daniel contacts in this chapter — see 1:20, where a king is brought an unreadable inscription — in an account whose subject is a king ruling a people whose language he could not at first understand.

links.note: 'Behold, I will speak unto you somewhat concerning Mosiah, which was made king over the land of Zarahemla.' Six consecutive words of Daniel 9:1, from the only KJV verse that uses the construction. Daniel 9:1 is a regnal dating formula introducing the chapter in which Daniel reads Jeremiah and prays over the seventy years; Omni 1:12 is a regnal introduction opening the account of a migration out of the land of Nephi. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and so not one of his quotations, but the run is unbroken and the phrase has no competitor in the KJV. The one caution is that this is a formula rather than a saying: a writer steeped in the KJV could reach for it without meaning Daniel, which is why the confidence is high and not certain.
links.text: In the first year of Darius the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, which was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans;

provenance.other: “being warned of God” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Matthew 2:12, Matthew 2:22, and Hebrews 11:7. All three are warnings to leave or to build against a coming destruction, and two of the three are in the flight into Egypt. The Book of Mormon reads 'warned of the Lord', which is in no KJV verse; the substitution of 'the Lord' for 'God' is the text's habit, not a departure from the source.
provenance.significance: Mosiah's departure is narrated in the words of Lehi's, and Lehi's was narrated in the words of Joseph's. 1 Nephi 2:2 has the Lord commanding Lehi to depart into the wilderness with his family, and that verse is already catalogued against Matthew 2:13. Omni 1:12 repeats the motion for the second founder: warned, flee, out of the land, into the wilderness, with as many as would hearken. The Book of Mormon's two exoduses are told with the same New Testament verse behind them, which makes Matthew 2 — not Exodus — the KJV passage that gives this book its departure-narrative grammar.

links.note: 'He being warned of the Lord that he should flee out of the land of Nephi.' Warned + flee out of a land is the shape of Matthew 2:12-13, where Joseph is 'warned of God in a dream' and told to 'flee into Egypt'; Matthew 2:22 repeats the participle for the return. The KJV's Old Testament never uses 'warned' of a divine instruction to depart — its verb is 'get thee out' (Genesis 12:1) or 'flee' with no warning clause. Hebrews 11:7 is named as a composite because it is the third occurrence and because the Book of Mormon has already been quarrying Hebrews 11 for its migration language (1 Nephi 2:20, 4:2). Moderate rather than high: the participle is shared but the object is changed, and 'flee out of the land' is not itself a KJV string.
links.text: And being warned of God in a dream that they should not return to Herod, they departed into their own country another way.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he did according as the Lord had commanded him. And they departed out of the land into the wilderness, as many as would hearken unto the voice of the Lord; and they were led by many preachings and prophesyings. And they were admonished continually by the word of God; and they were led by the power of his arm, through the wilderness, until they came down into the land which is called the land of Zarahemla.

provenance.other: “led them by” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 63:12. The KJV's other leading formulas are 'led them forth', 'led them out', and 'the LORD led them' with no instrument; the construction with 'by' plus a divine limb belongs to this verse.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 63:11-14 is the Old Testament's own retrospect on the Exodus, asked as a question by a later generation wondering where that God has gone: where is he that brought them up out of the sea, that led them by the right hand of Moses with his glorious arm, that led them through the deep as an horse in the wilderness? Omni 1:13 and 1:16 answer it as narrative. Mosiah's people 'were led by the power of his arm, through the wilderness'; the people of Zarahemla 'was brought by the hand of the Lord, across the great waters'. Both halves of Isaiah's question — the arm through the wilderness, the hand across the water — are distributed across the two migrations the chapter puts side by side, which is a tidier piece of construction than a colophon chapter is usually credited with.

links.note: 'They were led by the power of his arm, through the wilderness.' The distinctive elements are the passive leading, the divine arm as the instrument, and the wilderness, and Isaiah 63:12-13 is the only place in the KJV that holds all three: 'That led them by the right hand of Moses with his glorious arm … That led them through the deep, as an horse in the wilderness.' The Book of Mormon substitutes 'power' for 'glorious' and drops Moses, which is what the sentence needs — Mosiah is the Moses figure here and cannot also be the instrument. Moderate rather than high, because 'arm' as divine power is widespread in the KJV (Exodus 6:6, Deuteronomy 4:34, Isaiah 52:10) and only the 'led them by' collocation is rare.
links.text: That led them by the right hand of Moses with his glorious arm, dividing the water before them, to make himself an everlasting name?

pericopes.text: And they discovered a people, which was called the people of Zarahemla. Now, there was great rejoicing among the people of Zarahemla; and also, Zarahemla did rejoice exceedingly, because that the Lord had sent the people of Mosiah with the plates of brass which contained the record of the Jews.
Behold, it came to pass that Mosiah discovered that the people of Zarahemla, came out from Jerusalem, at the time that Zedekiah, king of Judah, was carried away captive into Babylon.

provenance.route: Jeremiah 39:9 → KJV → 1 Nephi 1:13 → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “carried away captive into Babylon” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 39:9. Modern versions render the same Hebrew as 'carried into exile' and share no wording with the Book of Mormon here. 'Zedekiah king of Judah' occurs in fifteen KJV verses, all but two in Jeremiah.
provenance.significance: The phrase was adjudicated at its first use, 1 Nephi 1:13, where it is part of Lehi's vision of the fall of Jerusalem; this row is recorded rather than passed over because Omni 1:15 does something the first use does not. It converts the phrase into a date. Amaleki has no interest in Zedekiah except as a clock: the people of Zarahemla left Jerusalem 'at the time that' the captivity happened, which is how the Book of Mormon synchronises its second, unrelated colony with the biblical record. The one point in the whole book where two migrations are pinned to each other is pinned by a KJV singleton.

links.note: 'At the time that Zedekiah, king of Judah, was carried away captive into Babylon.' Five continuous words from the KJV's only occurrence of the phrase. Jeremiah 39:9 is about Nebuzaradan deporting the remnant of the people, not about Zedekiah, who in that chapter is blinded and 'carried him to Babylon' in chains (39:7) — so the Book of Mormon has taken the phrase from one verse of the chapter and attached it to the king named two verses earlier. That is a reader's compression of Jeremiah 39, not a copy of it. Adjudicated in full at 1 Nephi 1:13; the row is kept here because Omni's use is a fresh application of the phrase in a new authorial voice and a different rhetorical function.
links.text: Then Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive into Babylon the remnant of the people that remained in the city, and those that fell away, that fell to him, with the rest of the people that remained.

pericopes.text: And they journied in the wilderness, and was brought by the hand of the Lord, across the great waters, into the land where Mosiah discovered them; and they had dwelt there from that time forth.

And at the time that Mosiah discovered them, they had become exceeding numerous. Nevertheless, they had had many wars and serious contentions, and had fallen by the sword from time to time; and their language had become corrupted; and they had brought no records with them and they denied the being of their Creator; and Mosiah, nor the people of Mosiah, could not understand them.

But it came to pass that Mosiah caused that they should be taught in his language. And it came to pass that after they were taught in the language of Mosiah, Zarahemla gave a genealogy of his fathers, according to his memory; and they are written, but not in these plates.
And it came to pass that the people of Zarahemla, and of Mosiah, did unite together; and Mosiah was appointed to be their king.

provenance.other: “appointed to be their” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The KJV normally says 'made him king', 'set a king over them', or 'anointed him king'; the passive 'appointed to be their <office>' is Nehemiah's alone.
provenance.significance: Nehemiah 5:14 is Nehemiah's account of the twelve years he was governor in Judah, and the point of the sentence is what he did not take: 'I and my brethren have not eaten the bread of the governor.' It is the KJV's set piece on a ruler who declines the perquisites of office over a people newly reassembled from two populations. Omni 1:19 is the moment the people of Zarahemla and the people of Mosiah 'did unite together' and a single king is set over the merged nation — and Benjamin, Mosiah's son, will make exactly Nehemiah's speech in Mosiah 2:12-14, that he has not sought gold or been supported by his people but has laboured with his own hands. If that later speech has a KJV model, Nehemiah 5 is it, and the vocabulary enters the book here.

links.note: 'And Mosiah was appointed to be their king.' The five-word run 'was appointed to be their' comes from the KJV's single instance of the construction, and the setting matches: a leader installed over a population that has just been consolidated in a land not originally its own. Moderate rather than high because the phrase is administrative rather than distinctive — a writer could produce it without a source — and because 'king' for 'governor' is the only content word changed. The reason to record it at all is forward-looking: Benjamin's renunciation of a king's living in Mosiah 2 is the closest thing in the Book of Mormon to Nehemiah 5:14-18, and this verse is where the phrasing first appears.
links.text: Moreover from the time that I was appointed to be their governor in the land of Judah, from the twentieth year even unto the two and thirtieth year of Artaxerxes the king, that is, twelve years, I and my brethren have not eaten the bread of the governor.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass in the days of Mosiah, there was a large stone brought unto him, with engravings on it; and he did interpret the engravings, by the gift and power of God.

provenance.other: The KJV has exactly two type-scenes of a king confronted with writing or a dream he cannot read and an interpreter given the meaning by God: Joseph before Pharaoh (Genesis 41) and Daniel before Belshazzar (Daniel 5). Only Daniel 5 involves an inscription on a hard surface, and only Daniel 5 has the sequence engraving → summoned interpreters who fail → interpretation given → a nation's destruction announced.
provenance.significance: Metalepsis, if the link holds. Recover Daniel 5 and the inscription's content is MENE MENE TEKEL UPHARSIN — a kingdom numbered and finished, weighed and found wanting, divided — delivered to a king in the night his city falls. The engraved stone brought to Mosiah reports 'one Coriantumr, and the slain of his people', a whole nation destroyed to its last survivor, who is then produced alive before the court that has just heard his epitaph. In Daniel the writing indicts the king who reads it; in Omni the writing indicts a people already dead, and the reading king is spared. The scene is Daniel 5 with the judgement displaced onto someone else — which is precisely what Omni 1:22's 'the severity of the Lord fell upon them, according to his judgments' says out loud.

links.note: 'There was a large stone brought unto him, with engravings on it; and he did interpret the engravings, by the gift and power of God.' There is almost no shared wording — 'interpret' and 'engravings' against Daniel's 'interpretation' and 'writing' — so this is filed as figural, and kjvSpecific is 'no' because there is nothing verbal to test. The case is the shape: a stone inscription nobody present can read, brought to a king, interpreted by divine gift, announcing the annihilation of a people. The KJV tells that story once. It is also the second Daniel contact in the chapter (see 1:12, six words of Daniel 9:1), which is worth weighing — a chapter that has already reached for Daniel's regnal formula reaching next for Daniel's inscription scene is a pattern, not two coincidences.
links.whyNot: Divine interpretation of an unknown script is a broad ancient topos and the Book of Mormon has its own well-developed apparatus for it (the interpreters, the seer). Mosiah's stone could be entirely internal to that apparatus, with Daniel supplying nothing. A cautious reader would decline the row; it is here because the pairing with 1:12 makes the Daniel presence in this chapter harder to dismiss than either instance alone.
links.text: And I have heard of thee, that thou canst make interpretations, and dissolve doubts: now if thou canst read the writing, and make known to me the interpretation thereof, thou shalt be clothed with scarlet, and have a chain of gold about thy neck, and shalt be the third ruler in the kingdom.

pericopes.text: And they gave an account of one Coriantumr, and the slain of his people. And Coriantumr was discovered by the people of Zarahemla; and he dwelt with them for the space of nine Moons.

It also spake a few words concerning his fathers. And his first parents came out from the Tower, at the time the Lord confounded the language of the people; and the severity of the Lord fell upon them, according to his judgments, which is just; and their bones lay scattered in the land northward.

provenance.other: “confound the language” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 11:9. The Book of Mormon's past tense, 'the Lord confounded the language of the people', occurs in no KJV verse and is a straightforward inflection of Genesis 11:9's infinitive. 'The Tower' as an absolute noun, capitalised in 1830, has no KJV parallel — Genesis 11:4-5 has 'a tower' and 'the tower'.
provenance.significance: This is the seam where the Book of Mormon splices a second people into Genesis. Omni 1:22 does not merely allude to Babel; it uses Genesis 11:9 as a datum, an event with a date, from which the Jaredite migration departs — 'his first parents came out from the Tower, at the time the Lord confounded the language of the people' — exactly as 1:15 uses Zedekiah's captivity as the date from which the people of Zarahemla depart. Two of the book's three founding migrations are pinned to Genesis 11 and Jeremiah 39 respectively, seven verses apart, by the same 'at the time that' construction. And Genesis 11:9's second clause supplies the consequence Omni turns to next: 'from thence did the LORD scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth' becomes 'their bones lay scattered in the land northward'.

links.note: 'His first parents came out from the Tower, at the time the Lord confounded the language of the people.' The KJV names the confounding of language once, at Genesis 11:9, and Omni takes the verb, its object, and its agent unchanged. Two verses earlier the chapter has already prepared the theme without the vocabulary — the people of Zarahemla 'their language had become corrupted', so that Mosiah 'could not understand them' (1:17) — which is Babel narrated as a consequence before it is named as a cause. The whole Jaredite record, which Ether will later unfold, is introduced in this chapter as a footnote to nine verses of Genesis.
links.text: Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth: and from thence did the LORD scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth.

provenance.other: “scatter your bones” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 6:5, and “bones are scattered” in exactly one, Psalm 141:7. The two are the KJV's only statements of unburied bones scattered over a landscape; Ezekiel's are scattered as a judgement executed by God, Psalm 141's as an image of the speaker's own distress.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 6 is the oracle against the mountains of Israel, where the scattering of bones round the altars is the proof of the sentence — 'and ye shall know that I am the LORD' closes the paragraph. Omni 1:22 has the same three-part structure in one clause: judgement pronounced ('the severity of the Lord fell upon them, according to his judgments, which is just'), and the bones on the ground as its residue. What the Book of Mormon adds is geography — 'in the land northward' — turning a prophetic image into a survey report, which is how the whole verse works: Genesis 11 as chronology, Ezekiel 6 as landscape.

links.note: 'And their bones lay scattered in the land northward.' Ezekiel 6:5 is the only KJV verse in which God scatters bones as an act of judgement, and Omni 1:22 places its scattered bones in exactly that logical position, as the consequence of 'his judgments'. Psalm 141:7 is recorded as the alternative because it holds the closer English string, but its sense is wrong — the psalmist's scattered bones are a complaint, not a verdict. Moderate: the collocation is common enough as an idea (Jeremiah 8:1-2, 2 Kings 23:14 both scatter bones out of graves) that no single verse is compelled, and only Ezekiel 6:5 fits the judgement frame Omni supplies.
links.text: And I will lay the dead carcases of the children of Israel before their idols; and I will scatter your bones round about your altars.

provenance.other: “severity” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 11:22, where it appears twice. The word is absent from the entire Old Testament in the KJV. Its Book of Mormon uses are few, and Omni 1:22 is among the earliest.
provenance.significance: The verb agrees as well as the noun. Romans 11:22 reads 'the goodness and severity of God: on them which fell, severity'; Omni reads 'the severity of the Lord fell upon them'. The Book of Mormon has taken Paul's noun and Paul's verb and reassigned the falling — in Romans the people fall and severity is what they meet, in Omni the severity falls and the people are what it meets. Romans 11 is already a working source for this book (the olive tree at 1 Nephi 10:12, the fulness of the Gentiles at 1 Nephi 15:13), which makes availability of the chapter to the text's idiom not in question; what is new here is that the severity half of Paul's antithesis, rather than the grafting half, is what gets used.

links.note: 'And the severity of the Lord fell upon them, according to his judgments, which is just.' The English word 'severity' enters the KJV in one verse only, and that verse pairs it with the verb 'fell' in the same sentence. Against a text that elsewhere says 'wrath', 'judgments', 'destruction', the choice of this word is worth noticing. Note the 1830 reading 'which is just' — a singular verb agreeing with 'severity' rather than with 'judgments' — which the 1920 edition corrected to 'are'; the first edition thus keeps the sentence focused on Paul's noun, and the modern text moves the focus to the judgements. Moderate, not high: the phrase 'the severity of the Lord' is not itself in the KJV, and a single rare noun is thin ground on its own.
links.text: Behold therefore the goodness and severity of God: on them which fell, severity; but toward thee, goodness, if thou continue in his goodness: otherwise thou also shalt be cut off.

pericopes.text: Behold, I, Amaleki, was born in the days of Mosiah; and I have lived to see his death; and Benjamin, his son, reigneth in his stead.

And behold, I have seen in the days of king Benjamin, a serious war, and much bloodshed, between the Nephites and the Lamanites. But behold, the Nephites did obtain much advantage over them; yea, insomuch that king Benjamin did drive them out of the land of Zarahemla.

And it came to pass that I began to be old; and, having no seed, and knowing king Benjamin to be a just man before the Lord, wherefore, I shall deliver up these plates unto him, exhorting all men to come unto God, the Holy One of Israel, and believe in prophesying, and in revelations, and in the ministering of Angels, and in the gift of speaking with tongues, and in the gift of interpreting languages in all things which is good: for there is nothing which is good, save it comes from the Lord; and that which is evil, cometh from the Devil.

provenance.other: “kinds of tongues” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “interpretation of tongues” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — the same verse, 1 Corinthians 12:10. Nowhere else in the Bible are tongues and their interpretation named as two separate gifts in one list.
provenance.significance: Amaleki's closing exhortation is a spiritual-gifts list, and its order is Paul's. Paul: prophecy, discerning of spirits, divers kinds of tongues, the interpretation of tongues. Amaleki: prophesying, revelations, the ministering of angels, the gift of speaking with tongues, the gift of interpreting languages. Three of the four Pauline items are in Pauline sequence, and the two rarest — tongues and their interpretation as distinct gifts, adjacent and in that order — are taken from the one verse in the Bible that makes that distinction. The substitution is the interesting part: Paul's 'interpretation of tongues' becomes 'interpreting languages', which is what Mosiah did to the engraved stone five verses earlier. The chapter has quietly redefined a charismatic gift as a philological one.

links.note: 'And believe in prophesying, and in revelations, and in the ministering of Angels, and in the gift of speaking with tongues, and in the gift of interpreting languages.' Both halves of the tongues pair are KJV singletons and both are in 1 Corinthians 12:10; the list around them keeps Paul's order. 'Ministering of angels' is not a KJV phrase — Hebrews 1:14's 'ministering spirits, sent forth to minister' is the nearest thing, and is named as a composite rather than as a source. The gift language itself ('the gift of') is Paul's throughout the chapter. Below any quotation threshold, since no clause is reproduced; the case is the rarity of the pair plus the retained sequence.
links.text: To another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discerning of spirits; to another divers kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues:

provenance.route: James 1:17 + 1 John 3:8 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “every good gift” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 1:17, and “is of the devil” in exactly one, 1 John 3:8. Between them they supply both halves of Omni's antithesis, and neither half has a competitor elsewhere in the Bible.
provenance.significance: Omni 1:25's closing sentence is the earliest statement in the Book of Mormon of a test that Moroni 7:12-17 will later expand into the book's fullest piece of moral epistemology — everything good is from God, everything evil from the devil, and a man may know the one from the other. That developed passage is generally read against James; this verse shows the same two New Testament verses already fused, in the same order, four hundred pages earlier and in a colophon rather than a sermon. Note also the immediate context: the sentence follows a list of spiritual gifts, which is exactly the setting in which James 1:17 makes its own claim about where gifts come from.

links.note: 'For there is nothing which is good, save it comes from the Lord; and that which is evil, cometh from the Devil.' Two KJV singletons welded into an antithesis the KJV never states as one. James 1:17 gives the positive half — every good gift is from above, and 'cometh down' supplies Omni's verb — and 1 John 3:8 the negative, 'he that committeth sin is of the devil'. Moderate rather than high: neither half reproduces a clause, and the good/evil, God/devil polarity is common enough theologically that a writer need not have had either verse open. What raises it above an echo is the verb 'cometh', which is James's, carried over into the half of the sentence that belongs to John.
links.text: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.

pericopes.text: And now, my beloved brethren, I would that ye should come unto Christ, which is the Holy One of Israel, and partake of his salvation, and the power of his redemption. Yea, come unto him, and offer your whole souls as an offering unto him, and continue in fasting and praying, and endure to the end; and as the Lord liveth, ye will be saved.

provenance.other: “living sacrifice” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 12:1, and “fasting and prayer” in exactly one, 1 Corinthians 7:5. The KJV never speaks of offering a soul; its offerings are bodies (Romans 12:1), beasts, and 'the sacrifices of God' which are 'a broken spirit' (Psalm 51:17).
provenance.significance: Romans 12:1 asks for the body and calls it a living sacrifice; Omni 1:26 asks for 'your whole souls as an offering unto him'. The exchange is not neutral. Paul's whole point is that the thing offered stays alive, and the Book of Mormon keeps the paradox while moving it from the flesh to the soul — which is the direction its own anthropology runs. The verse also stands where Romans 12:1 stands, at the hinge from doctrine to exhortation: Amaleki has just finished his historical record and turns, in the last thing he writes, to what his readers should do. Compare Hays on metalepsis — 'I beseech you therefore, brethren' is Paul's cue that the argument is over and the appeal has begun, and 'And now, my beloved brethren, I would that ye should come unto Christ' is Amaleki's.

links.note: 'Yea, come unto him, and offer your whole souls as an offering unto him, and continue in fasting and praying.' The offering of the self as a living thing rather than a slain one is Romans 12:1's distinctive move, and 'whole souls' answers Paul's 'bodies'. 'Fasting and prayer' as a fixed pair occurs once in the KJV, at 1 Corinthians 7:5, and is named as a composite — the Book of Mormon's participial 'fasting and praying' is its own inflection. Moderate: no clause is reproduced, and both offering-language and fasting are widely available. The row is worth taking under CONVENTIONS §0a because the substitution of soul for body is a legible, arguable act of reading rather than a coincidence of vocabulary.
links.text: I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.

provenance.route: Matthew 10:22 → KJV → 1 Nephi 22:31 → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “endureth to the end” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 10:22; “endure unto the end” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 24:13 and Mark 13:13. The Book of Mormon's fixed form is 'endure to the end', which matches Matthew 10:22's preposition against the other two.
provenance.significance: The preposition is the whole finding, and it is small. Matthew 10:22 and Mark 13:13 say almost the same sentence, but Matthew 10:22 has 'endureth to the end' where the Olivet parallels have 'endure unto the end'. Every Book of Mormon occurrence of the formula, from 1 Nephi 13:37 onward, reads 'to the end' and never 'unto the end' — so the book has, consistently and without exception, taken the missionary-discourse form rather than the apocalyptic one. Omni 1:26 is one of the places that consistency can be tested, and it holds.

links.note: 'And continue in fasting and praying, and endure to the end; and as the Lord liveth, ye will be saved.' Adjudicated at first use in 1 Nephi 13:37 and again at 22:31; recorded here because the formula is doing structural work — it closes the book of Omni, and with it the small plates. What Omni adds is the oath: the KJV's promise is conditional ('he that endureth to the end shall be saved'), and Amaleki converts it into a guaranteed second-person outcome sworn on the life of the Lord. The clause 'as the Lord liveth' is itself a KJV formula, and its collision with Matthew 10:22 here is registered as an exclusion at this verse rather than as a link, because the nearest KJV parallel says the opposite.
links.text: And ye shall be hated of all men for my name’s sake: but he that endureth to the end shall be saved.

pericopes.text: And now, I would speak somewhat concerning a certain number which went up into the wilderness, to return to the land of Nephi: for there was a large number which were desirous to possess the land of their inheritance;

wherefore, they went up into the wilderness. And their leader being a strong and a mighty man, and a stiffnecked man, wherefore, he caused a contention among them; and they were all slain, save fifty, in the wilderness, and they returned again to the land of Zarahemla.
And it came to pass that they also took others, to a considerable number, and took their journey again into the wilderness.

And I, Amaleki, had a brother, which also went with them; and I have not since known concerning them. And I am about to lay down in my grave; and these plates are full. And I make an end of my speaking.

variants: 1830 'lay down in my grave' → 1920 'lie down in my grave'

provenance.other: “go down into the grave” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 37:35, and the KJV's other descent-to-the-grave idioms — 'go down to the grave' (Genesis 42:38, 44:29, 44:31, Job 7:9), 'bring down to the grave' — cluster in the same Joseph narrative. The Book of Mormon's 'lay down in my grave' is in no KJV verse; the 1920 edition changed 'lay' to 'lie', which moves the phrase toward standard English and no closer to any source.
provenance.significance: Read the two sentences together and the sequence is the argument. 'And I, Amaleki, had a brother, which also went with them; and I have not since known concerning them. And I am about to lay down in my grave.' Genesis 37:35 is Jacob refusing comfort for a son who has vanished into the wilderness and is presumed dead: 'For I will go down into the grave unto my son mourning.' Amaleki, childless and the last of his line, records the disappearance of a brother into the wilderness and then, in the next clause, his own descent to the grave. Neither text mentions the other; the placement does the work.

links.note: Amaleki's closing colophon. The phrase itself has been softened away from any KJV wording — the KJV goes down into the grave, Amaleki lays down in his. What makes the echo worth recording is that the sentence before it supplies Genesis 37's situation exactly: a brother gone into the wilderness with a company, never heard of again, and a survivor who turns immediately to his own death. Filed as an echo, not an allusion, because the verbal contact is a single reworked idiom.
links.whyNot: 'Grave' and the descent into it are among the commonest images in the KJV's poetic books, and a dying scribe saying he is about to be buried needs no source at all. The 1830 'lay' rather than 'lie' weakens the verbal case further, since the KJV's Joseph verses all use 'go down'. The link is recorded for the narrative coincidence in the preceding clause, and a reader who takes that as accidental should decline it.
links.text: And all his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him; but he refused to be comforted; and he said, For I will go down into the grave unto my son mourning. Thus his father wept for him.
